parole.significato: -y, -ery, -able, -ible; used to form adjectives from verbs denoting action, etc.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ibilis, -ēbilis, which displaced -ābilis. The sound change from Latin [ɪ, eː] to [o] appears to have been due to the velarizing influence of the following [ɫ] in early Tuscan. Compare Montauto (from montem altum “tall mountain”) or topo (from talpa “mole”). Doublet of -ibile, w

parole.significato: tutor, especially one hired by a wealthy family
parole.testo: Feminine of aio, presumed to be from the unattested Gothic *𐌷𐌰𐌲𐌾𐌰 (*hagja), or from Latin avia. Compare Sicilian aju, Spanish ayo.
From a- + lungo + -are or from a Vulgar Latin root *allongāre, from ad + Late Latin longāre (cf. also elongāre), from Latin longus. Compare French allonger.
Probably from Vulgar Latin *alima, dissimilated form of Latin anima (compare Spanish and Portuguese alma); alternatively, a borrowing from Old Occitan (compare Occitan anma, arma). Doublet of anima.
From amaro + -ezza, or from a Vulgar Latin *amāritia, from Latin amāritiēs.

Probably from a- + mazza (“club, baton”) + -are, or alternatively possibly related to Latin mactāre, through a Vulgar Latin root *mactiāre, although this is less likely. Compare Sicilian ammazzari, Spanish mazar, Portuguese maçar, Occitan massar, Romansh mazzar, Venetan masar, Friulian maçâ, Istriot

parole.significato: Anglicism (word or other feature originating in the English language)
parole.testo: From ànglico + -ìsmo. Calque of English Anglicism and French anglicisme.

From Latin antea, with the -i under influence of Italian anti (“before, in front of”) (from Latin ante) or from Latin antesic (from Latin ante + sic and used in the Peregrinatio Egeriae), or from a Vulgar Latin *antius, as a neuter comparative of ante. Compare Old French ains, Catalan ans. See also
Possibly from Ancient Greek ἄρῐστος (árĭstos, “the best”), as it is considered the most prized cut of pig meat or from Latin arista (“edge”) since it is the pork's back cut.

parole.significato: to drizzle, to wet slightly (as if with dew)
parole.testo: Either inherited or borrowed from Old Occitan arozar or Old French arroser; in all cases from Vulgar Latin *arrosāre, itself from Latin adrorō. First attested before 1250.
Borrowed from Occitan artelh, or from Old French arteil, in either case from Latin articulus. Doublet of articolo.

parole.significato: to besiege, to lay siege to
parole.testo: Perhaps a learned borrowing from Medieval Latin assediāre, reshaping of Classical Latin obsidēre. Alternatively, derived from assedio (“siege”) + -are (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix).
From a- + sottile (“thin”) + -are, or from a- + sottigliare (now obsolete), from Late Latin subtiliāre, from Latin subtīlis.

parole.significato: to equip, to fit out, to tool up
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from attrezzo, itself possibly from French attraits. Alternatively from Vulgar Latin *attrectiāre, from Latin attrectāre.
From Latin vīvācius, comparative form of vīvāciter (“vigorously”), from vīvāx (“vigorous, lively”). Compare Catalan aviat. Alternatively from Latin vīvāciter.
From balza or possibly a Vulgar Latin root *balteanus, from Latin balteus. Compare also Old French bauçant.

From Medieval Latin bombacium, Byzantine Greek βαμβάκιον (bambákion), from either Ancient Greek βάμβαξ (bámbax, “cotton”) or Ancient Greek βόμβυξ (bómbux, “silk-worm”), whose ultimate origin is unknown. Compare Greek βαμβάκι (vamváki), Venetan bonbaxo, Middle Persian pmbk' (pambag).
Possibly inherited from Vulgar Latin *bastōnem, itself a modification of Late Latin bastum, or possibly noun use of the verb *bastō, from Ancient Greek βαστάζω (bastázō). Compare French bâton.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; alternatively; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Probably from either Proto-Germanic *bukkaz, *bukkô (“male goat”) or Proto-Celtic *bukkos, whence French bouc. The -e- is most readily explained through the Middle High German plural böcke (early on also unrounded; compare contemporary Bavarian Beck). Alternatively from Latin ībex, though

Inherited from Old Italian biastema, from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin blasphēmia (remodeled after the verb bestemmiare, or alternatively through a Vulgar Latin form *blastemia), from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía).
From Latin betōnica or ve(t)tōnica, from Vettones, a people in Lusitania of possible Celtic origin, either Gaulish, Celtiberian, or Hispano-Celtic. Compare French bétoine, Spanish betónica.

parole.significato: glass (drinking vessel), cup, tumbler (glass without stem)
parole.testo: From Late Latin bīcārium (cf. also Old French bichier, pichier, compare modern French pichet, English beaker, pitcher, German Becher, Dutch beker), itself possibly from bacarium, or from Ancient Greek βῖκος (bîkos).
Of germanic origin. Most probably from either Middle High German bloß or Middle Low German blott.
Probably from Old French bouton, from the verb bouter, or alternatively possibly from Vulgar Latin *bottonem or *botonus.

From Vulgar Latin *bottia, a Germanic borrowing, from Frankish *boce (“knob”), from Old High German bozzan (“to beat”), from Proto-West Germanic *bautan (“to push, strike”). Compare French bosse, Occitan bossa; also Romanian bot. Alternatively, a northern variant of Italian boccia, from a Latin root

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; or possibly; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Probably from Vulgar Latin *bravus, from a fusion of Latin prāvus and barbarus. Less likely from Provençal brau (“show-off”), from Gaulish *bragos (compare Middle Irish breagha (modern breá) 'fine', Breton braga 'to strut'). Or perhaps borrowed from a descendant of Proto-Germanic *hrawaz
The origin is uncertain. Could be from Catalan brisa, influenced by rezze. Alternatively, from Vulgar Latin *brevidia, derived from a word which gave rise to Italian breva.
From Vulgar Latin *brocca, from either Ancient Greek πρόχοος (prókhoos, “vessel for water”), or from βροχίς (brokhís, “inkwell”), with influence from broccus. Further a cognate to Albanian prokë.

Attestions begin in northern Italy, and include bronzo in a Latin context in Liber consuetudinum Mediolani (1216); Lombard bronz, bronzo in Liber di Tre Scricciur, 1274; Venetan brondi ? in a semi-Latin document from Verona, 1339. Immediately, possibly from Latin *brundium, or directly from Latin br

From a Vulgar Latin *brusiāre, itself of uncertain origin; possibly from a form *prustiāre < *per-ust(u)lāre, from Latin per + ustulāre (compare perurere), or alternatively from a corruption of *combustulāre, from a change of prefix of ambustulāre, influenced by combustus; see ambūrēre. However, an

From the verb bucare, from buca, or from either Old Frankish *būk (“cavity, stomach”) or Gothic *𐌱𐌿𐌺𐍃 (*būks), both from Proto-Germanic *būkaz (“belly, torso”). Compare Occitan/Catalan buc ("torso; cow's chest"). More at bouk.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *burius (“red, dark”), either from Latin burrus (“reddish-brown”) or, less likely, from Latin furvus (“dark, dusky”).
From English bunker, or from German Bunker.

Traditionally believed to derive from Latin būris (“beam of the plow”), used by farmers and thus associated with countryside people; alternatively, perhaps, from Lombardic būr (“peasant”). Either way suffixed with -ino.

Perhaps from Ancient Greek βοτήρ (botḗr, “herdsman”), akin to βόσκω (bóskō, “to graze”). Alternatively from Ancient Greek βούτης (boútēs, “yokel”), from βοῦς (boûs, “cattle”). Caix derives it from Vulgar Latin puttulus, diminutive of puttus, from Latin putus (“boy”), since the meaning is still prese
From cacio (“cheese”) + cavallo (“horse”), inherited from Old Italian. More likely calqued from Neapolitan, or Sicilian casucavaḍḍu (or from dialectal cascavaḍḍu). Doublet of cosacavaddu.
Borrowed from Byzantine Greek καλαϕατέω (kalaphatéō) or from Arabic قَلْفَطَ (qalfaṭa, “to caulk (a ship)”), both from Latin calefaciō (“to heat”).
From caldara (cf. caldaia), with the suffix -one, or from a derivative of Latin caldarium, Late Latin caldaria. Compare French chaudron, Portuguese caldeirão, Spanish calderón.
From caldo or from a Vulgar Latin root *caldūra, from Latin caldus, calidus. Compare Romanian căldură.

Deverbal from cambiare + -o. From verb cambiare inherited from Vulgar Latin cambiāre (“to change, exchange”) from Late Latin cambiō, or from corresponding noun Latin cambium (“change”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *kh₂emp- (“to bend, curve”). Compare Spanish cambio and Portuguese câmbio.
From cancello + -iere, or from Late Latin cancellārius, from Latin cancellus. Cognate with Sicilian canciḍḍeri.
Borrowed from Spanish caramelo or French caramel, from Portuguese caramelo, itself either from Late Latin calamellus, or Medieval Latin cannamellis.

parole.significato: complexion (appearance of the skin on the face)
parole.testo: From carne or from a Late Latin carnātiōnem, from Latin carō.
From catena (“chain, bond”) + -accio, or from Late Latin catēnāceum, from Latin catēna.
Probably borrowed from Portuguese cabo or from Genoese, ultimately from Latin capulum.

parole.significato: to hoop (put hoops around a barrel, etc.)
parole.testo: From cerchio + -are, or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin *circlāre < Late Latin circulāre, from Latin circulārī, and therefore doublet of the borrowing circolare. Compare French cercler.

Of unknown origin shared with Spanish zapato and French sabot and savate and Sicilian savatta. Possibly from Tatar чабата (çabata, “overshoes”), ultimately either from Ottoman Turkish چاپوت (çaput, çapıt, “patchwork, tatters”), from Ottoman Turkish چاپمق (çapmak, “to slap on”), or of Iranian origin,
From Vulgar Latin or Late Latin īsicia, plural of īsicium (“minced meat”), from īnsicium < Latin īnsecō (“cut up”). Compare Spanish chicha. Alternatively, from a syncope of carniccia.

From the variant ciriegia, from Vulgar Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of Late Latin ceresium, from Latin cerasium, from Ancient Greek κεράσιον (kerásion, “cherry”), from κερασός (kerasós, “bird cherry”), ultimately possibly of Anatolian origin. Alternatively from ciliegio, ciriegio (Tuscan),

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; alternatively; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps of Germanic origin; cf. German Schutt (“rubble”). Alternatively from Latin cautēs (“rough pointed rock”), via a Gallo-Italic language (hence the palatalization of /ka-/) with a change in gender and notable reduction in size. Either way, cognate with Romagnol ẓòt.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Several theories exist. Possibly from a central-northern Italian word (cf. cocón) ultimately derived from Latin calcāre (“to press”), or from a derivative of Latin caucus, from Ancient Greek káukē. Alternatively, from a corchiume, related to Spanish corcho (cf. English cork), from Latin c
From comprare + -tore, or from Late Latin comparātōrem, from Latin comparō.

From Late Latin conredum, from cum (“with”) + redum (“preparation, arrangement”), which is of Germanic origin; see also Dutch reden, Gothic *𐍂𐌴𐌳𐌰𐌽 (*rēdan), 𐍂𐌰𐌹𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (raidjan), all from Proto-Germanic *rēdaną (“to advise, decide”). Alternatively back-formation of corredare, compare arredare (“to equi

parole.significato: a hook, especially one used for fishing for tuna
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French croc, from Frankish *krōk (“hook”) or from Old Norse krókr (“hook, bend, bight”), both from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“hook”), from Proto-Indo-European *gerg- (“tracery, basket, twist”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; perhaps; or from; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps from a Vulgar Latin *dadu, itself either from Latin datum (“thrown, given”), or from Arabic أَعْدَاد (ʔaʕdād, “numbers”). Compare Spanish and Portuguese dado, Catalan dau, French dé (whence English die).

From Medieval Latin or Late Latin dentālis, derived from Latin dēns (“tooth”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dénts, *h₃dónts. By surface analysis, dent(e) (“tooth”) + -ale (“-al”, adjectival derivational suffix).
From Latin diatonicus or from French diatonique.

From a Vulgar Latin derivative of Latin ieiūnium. The initial Latin ie- or je- may have changed to de- over time, leading to di- in Italian. Compare the similar Catalan dejuni. Alternatively digiuno may have been regressively derived from the verb digiunare, and was independent of this Latin word.

From Old High German grīnan (“to twist the mouth”) (whence English grin and French grincer (“to squeak, to gnash”)), from Proto-Germanic *grīnaną, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to rub, to grind”). di- used either to represent downward motion or as an intensifier.

parole.significato: to issue, to put out, to release, to disseminate (an invitation, press release, etc.)
parole.testo: From di- + ramo, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *dērāmāre, from Latin rāmus (“branch”). Compare Romanian dărâma, Dalmatian dramur, Old French deramer, Spanish and Portuguese derramar; compare also Albanian dërmoj.

Probably a back-formation of doccione (“conduit, spout”), from Latin ductiōnem, from ducere, infinitive of dūcō (“lead, guide; draw, pull”), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin root *ducea, ultimately from the same root. Compare Dozza, a borrowing from Emilian Dòza.
From doglia + -oso or from a Vulgar Latin root *doliōsus, from Latin dolor. Compare Romanian duios, Friulian duliôs.

Contraction/syncopation of diritto, from Vulgar Latin *dērēctus (or from Late Latin drictus; compare French droit, Catalan dret, Romanian drept, Sicilian drittu), from Latin dīrēctus. Doublet of diretto.

Uncertain, but several theories have been proposed: * It may derive from Sicilian facchinu (“jurist called upon to settle disputes related to customs”), ultimately from Arabic فَقِيه (faqīh, “theologian, jurisconsult, faqih”). According to this theory, the word originally referred to a customs offic
From Latin phaseolus, probably from Ancient Greek φάσηλος (phásēlos) or from Ancient Greek φασούλια (phasoúlia). Unrelated to fava.

parole.significato: to fail to germinate (of a seed)
parole.testo: From fallo + -are or falla + -are, from Vulgar Latin *falla, or from Late Latin fallāre, from Latin fallere.

Perhaps from Old Italian parpaglione, from Latin papiliō (“butterfly”). Compare Old French paveillon, Catalan papalló, Provençal parpalhos, Lombard parpaja. The f is difficult to account for, though it might be due to the Tuscan gorgia. Alternatively, from the dialectal Arabic word in Maltese farfet

Inherited from Latin forficula (“small scissors”), from forfic- (“scissors”) + -ula, with an unexpected shift of the first vowel. Compare borrowed doublet forficula and seemingly inherited doublet forfecchia (“earwig”). Alternatively, possibly from the Osco-Umbrian substrate, from Proto-Italic *farð
Either borrowed from Latin pharmacum, or from its source, Ancient Greek φάρμακον (phármakon).

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Possibly; perhaps; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Maybe from Old French felpe, feupe, of uncertain origin, but possibly from Late Latin faluppa (“straw, fiber, chip”) (perhaps of Germanic origin and borrowed from Frankish *felt), or from earlier ferpe, metathesized from fibra.
Borrowed from Occitan fermalh or from French fermail, in either case from Vulgar Latin *firmāc(u)lum, derived from Latin firmāre (“make fast”).
From ferro (“iron”) + -are, or from a Late Latin ferrāre (cf. Classical Latin ferrātus), from Latin ferrum. Compare French ferrer, Catalan and Portuguese ferrar, Spanish herrar.
Inherited from Latin fābula (> ˈfabla > 'fabbja > ˈfjabᵇa), or alternatively through a Vulgar Latin form *flaba from metathesis of *fabla. Doublet of favola and fola.
Uncertain, either derived from filo or, perhaps, from an unattested earlier *filzella, from Vulgar Latin *filicella, from Latin fīlum

parole.significato: phobia (irrational or obsessive fear or anxiety)
parole.testo: Noun use of the suffix -fobia, from Ancient Greek -φοβῐ́ᾱ (-phobĭ́ā), combining form of φόβος (phóbos, “fear”).

From forno + -ello (“diminutive suffix”), or from Vulgar Latin *furnellus, from Latin furnus. Compare French fourneau, Sicilian furneddu, Catalan fornell, Romansh furnel, Sardinian furredhu, Occitan fornèl, Portuguese fornilho, Spanish hornillo.

parole.significato: to shred, to rip into pieces
parole.testo: Borrowed from Old French frapper, fraper, or from Vulgar Latin frappāre; both from Frankish *hrapōn (“to jerk; snatch”).
From fritto + -ura, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *frīctūra, from Latin frīctus. Compare French friture, Romanian friptură, Spanish and Portuguese fritura, Sicilian frittura.
From fumo + -aiolo, or from Late Latin fūmāriolum, from Latin fūmārium, from fūmus.

From Middle French gaffe, from Old Occitan gaf (“hook”), derivative of gafar (“to seize”), either from Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍆- (gaf-), preterite stem of 𐌲𐌹𐌱𐌰𐌽 (giban, “to give”) or from 𐌲𐌰𐍆𐌰𐌷 (gafah, “clasp”), from 𐌲𐌰- (ga-) (intensifier) + 𐍆𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (fahan, “to catch”).

Possibly of Germanic origin, or from Latin vagus (“wandering, flighty, giddy”); likely of the same genesis as Old Occitan gai, whence cognate to French gai, Portuguese gaio and English gay. Cognate with Sicilian javiu.

Borrowed from Old High German garwi (“dress; equipment; preparation”), from Proto-Germanic *garwijaną (“to prepare”). More at garb. Alternatively, perhaps borrowed from Arabic قَالِب (qālib, “model, outline”), from Persian کالب (kâlob, “form, mold”), from Ancient Greek κᾱλοπόδιον (kālopódion, “shoem

parole.significato: cuckoopint, arum (Arum genus and species, especially Arum maculatum)
parole.testo: Unknown. The only attestation in Latin presents it as Gaulish: c. 400, Marcellus Empiricus, De medicamentis, 10:58: Polypum emendat herba proserpinalis, quae Graece draconteum, Gallice gigarus appellatur, vel sucus eius naribus infundatur vel si papyrus inde infecta et spicillo involuta naribus inse
From giudicare (“to judge”) + -mento (“-ment”), or possibly from Late Latin iūdicāmentum, from Latin iūdicō. Compare Spanish juzgamiento, Portuguese julgamento, Catalan jutjament, French jugement.
From gocciare or from a Vulgar Latin *guttia or *guttea; ultimately from Latin gutta.

From gargozza, or gargozzo, itself from an onomatopoeic root garg- or from Vulgar Latin *gurgutia or *gargutium. Another etymology proposed is *guttium, variant of Latin guttur (“throat”), confused with guttus (“jug”). Alternatively, possibly from a derivative Vulgar Latin *gusia (compare French gos
Probably from grovigliolo, from an alteration of rubiglio. Or possibly connected with Latin globus via a Vulgar Latin *globilia.
Possibly from a Vulgar Latin gruma, from Latin grumus, or alternatively of Germanic origin.
Perhaps from Proto-Germanic *wai (“expression of grief”). Alternatively from Ancient Greek οὐαί (ouaí), from the verse in Revelation 8:13. Compare English woe, German Weh, Latin vae.

Possibly borrowed from Old French gaschier, gacher, gasser (“to soil, spoil, waste”) and gaschier, guaschier, waschier (“to wash, soak”), both from Old Dutch *wascan, *wascon, from Frankish *waskan (“to wash, bathe”), from Proto-Germanic *waskaną (“to wash”), from Proto-Indo-European *wod- (“wet”).
From im (“in”) + bocca (“mouth”) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *imbuccāre, from Latin bucca. Compare Spanish and Catalan embocar, French emboucher, Romanian îmbuca.

Deverbal from ingombrare + -o. Or formed directly from the prefix in- with an uncertain stem (compare English cumber), either: * the Old French combre (“wooden obstacles on a river; dam”), combrer (“to hinder”); see modern French encombrer;  or * directly from the Latin cumulus (“an accumulation, a

parole.significato: to turn green, to green, to make green
parole.testo: Either from in- + verde + -ire, or from a Vulgar Latin *invir(i)dire, from *invir(i)descere, from Latin viridēscere. Compare Romanian înverzi, Catalan enverdir, Spanish enverdir, enverdecer, Portuguese enverdecer, French verdir.
From lavare + -tura, or from a Vulgar Latin *lavatūra, from Latin lavō. Compare French lavure, Sicilian lavatura, Spanish lavadura, Romanian lături.

From a Vulgar Latin *liccāre (compare French lécher), itself probably from Proto-West Germanic *likkōn. See English lick for more. Alternatively from an early contraction of *ligicāre, denasalized from *lingicāre, from Classical Latin lingere. This is based on the analogy with *fīccāre (whence Itali

From the older form lecconerìa, either from leccare (“lick”, verb), or from Old High German lecchari or lecchōn, from Ancient Greek λιχνεία (likhneía, “gluttony; greed”), related to λείχω (leíkhō, “lick up”). Cognate with Latin lingō (“lick”, verb)and German lecker (“tasty”).

From Latin iūlius, through a process of dissimilation; compare also the obsolete regional variant form giuglio. Alternatively, derived from a Vulgar Latin root *lūlius, along with other Italo-Romance and Rhaeto-Romance cognates; compare Corsican lugliu, Neapolitan lùglio, Sicilian lugghiu, Venetan l

parole.significato: a charge consisting of four crescents arrranged in a ring
parole.testo: Borrowed either from Spanish lunel or directly from French lunel, ultimately based on Latin lūna (“moon”).
Borrowed from Old French madrier or from Old Occitan madier, ultimately from Vulgar Latin *māterium, from Latin māteria (“matter; timber”).
From Latin mānsiōnem, either inherited or borrowed from Old French maison.

parole.significato: to be lacking, to be missing (of objects)
parole.testo: From manco (adjective) + -are, or from a Vulgar Latin *mancāre, from Latin mancus.

parole.significato: brand, make or trademark (of a commercial product)
parole.testo: Of Germanic origin, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *marką or Proto-Germanic *markō.
From Late Latin martellus, diminutive of martulus, variant of Latin marculus, diminutive of marcus, or from malleus (“hammer”). Compare Portguese martelo and Catalan martell.
Inherited from Late Latin mascara, *mascra, masca. Doublet of mascara.

From Late Latin mātrīnea, from māter (“mother”) + -īneus (“relative suffix”). Compare Late Latin mātrīna (“stepmother, godmother”); alternatively from Late Latin mātrigna, after the model of prīvignus (“stepson”).

From Late Latin mattus (“drunk, intoxicated”), itself either from a contraction of a form *madĭtus (as a past participle of Latin madeō), or madidus (“drunk, tipsy”). Cognate to French mat (“matte, pale”).
From minuzzare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiālia, from Latin minūtia. Compare Friulian minuçae, Old French menuisaille, Portuguese miuçalha, Aromanian minutsalji.
From minuzza /minuzzare + -ame or from a Vulgar Latin *minūtiamen, from Latin minūtia.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Unknown; Possibly; either; modello unc/uncertain
parole.significato: mozzetta (short cape with a hood worn by senior clergy)
parole.testo: Etymology uncertain, possibly either: * from mozzo (“cut off; shortened”, adjective) (from Vulgar Latin *mutius, from Latin mutilus (“mutilated”); further etymology uncertain, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *mewt- (“cut short”)); or * from Late Latin almucia (“hood or cape with a hood worn by cle

From Latin mūtulus, syncopated to *mutlus, or from cumulus, transposed to a Vulgar Latin form *muculus > *muclus. Based on the first etymology, mutulo is a doublet, and based on the second, cumulo and cumolo are.

Uncertain; either from Vulgar Latin *nīdiculāre (“to stay in one's nest”), from Latin nīdus (“nest”), or from Vulgar Latin *hinnitulāre, from Latin hinniō (“to neigh, whinny”), possibly even from a merger of the two.

From the feminine of the past participle of offrire, or from Medieval Latin or Late Latin offerta, ultimately from Latin offerō. Compare Spanish, Portuguese, Catalan, and Sardinian oferta; Friulian ufierte; Romansh offerta; Sicilian ufferta.
From Latin olīva, from Etruscan 𐌄𐌋𐌄𐌉𐌅𐌀 (eleiva) or from Proto-Hellenic *elaíwā (compare Mycenaean Greek 𐀁𐀨𐀷 (e-ra-wa), Ancient Greek ἐλαίᾱ (elaíā)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁loywom.
From oliva or from Vulgar Latin olīvus, from Latin olīva, olīvum.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; Probably; or from; either
parole.testo: Either from Old French page or from the same origin, from Late Latin pagius, of uncertain origin, probably from Ancient Greek παιδίον (paidíon, “boy, lad”), from παῖς (paîs, “child”); some sources consider this unlikely and suggest instead Latin pagus (“countryside”), in sense of "boy from the rural
Feminine of palombo or from Vulgar Latin palumba, from Latin palumbus.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain, but probably from the older variant palanco or from palanca, from Vulgar Latin palanca, from Latin phalanga, from Ancient Greek φάλαγξ (phálanx), or alternatively from a Vulgar Latin paranchus, palanchus. Cognate with Sicilian parànculu.

From Late Latin patrīneus, from pater (“father”) + -īneus (“relative suffix”). Compare Medieval Latin patrīnus (“godfather”); alternatively from Late Latin patrignus, after the model of prīvignus (“stepson”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Probably; perhaps; alternatively; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Perhaps a Lombardic or Carolingian era borrowing from Old High German barrezzen (“to hate”) or maybe from French page (“page, serving boy”), probably via Neapolitan pazzo (compare French adage “être effronté comme un page”). Alternatively from Latin patiēns (“suffering”). Compare Sicilian

Probably from Vulgar Latin *pedinus, a derivative of Latin pedem (“foot”). Compare Sicilian pèdinu, Romanian piedin, Albanian pedim. Alternatively from Latin pendulus. Less likely linked to penna / pinna (“feather”).
From penzolo + -are or from Vulgar Latin *pendiolāre, from *pendiolus, from Latin pendulus, from pendō.
Borrowed from Occitan perilh or French péril, in either case from Latin perīculum, from the Proto-Indo-European root *per- (“to go forth, forwards”). Doublet of pericolo.

Probably from Latin petīgō ("scab, eruption"), a popular form of impetīgo (perhaps through a Vulgar Latin root *peticla < *(im)peticula, or alternatively, from a Vulgar Latin *pestic(u)la, from pestis. Less likely from Ancient Greek πιττάκια (pittákia), plural of πιττάκιον (pittákion).
Either from an onomatopoeic root or from Lombardic (s)pizza, from Proto-Germanic *spitjaz, related to *spitō (“spike”), whence German Spitze (“peak”).

parole.significato: henhouse, chicken coop, chicken run, roost
parole.testo: From pollo + -aio, or from Late Latin pullārium, from Latin pullārius (“pertaining to young animals or chicks”), from pullus (“young animal, chick”). Compare also pollario.

parole.significato: In the Roman Empire, the tract of land denoting the formal, sacral ambit of a Roman city
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin pōmoerium, pōmērium (“the religious boundary of a city”), which word being either formed as post (“behind”) + moerus, mūrus (“wall”) + -ium (neuter form of -ius, adjectival suffix) or derived from Etruscan [Term?].
From pomo + -eto or from Late Latin pomētum, from Latin pomus. Compare Romanian pomet.
Either deverbal from provare (“to try; to test; to prove; to feel”) + -a, or from Late Latin proba, from Latin probō.
From pugno, or from a Vulgar Latin *pūgnālis, from Latin pugnus. Compare Spanish puñal, Portuguese punhal, Catalan punyal, French poignard (Old French poignal).
Uncertain. Possibly * from Arabic رَقَّاص (raqqāṣ, “courier, delivery boy”). * alternatively, from Ancient Greek ῥάκος (rhákos, “rag, tatter”, suggesting the clothing).

parole.significato: flagship of a fleet personally commanded by a king or viceroy (pre-18th c.)
parole.testo: Either borrowed from Old French reial, from Latin rēgālis (“regal, royal”), or inherited from Latin rēgālis with possible influence from French. Doublet of regale.
From Old French rihote, perhaps related to riboter or from Latin rugiō (“to roar”).

parole.significato: to restore, to turn around, to balance, to reorganize
parole.testo: From ri- + sanare, or from Late Latin resānāre, from Latin sānāre. Compare Spanish resanar.

parole.significato: to twist again, to retwist (wire, etc.)
parole.testo: From ri- + torcere (“to twist”), or from Vulgar Latin *retorcere, from Latin retorquēre.

Perhaps from Latin aerūginem (“rust”), from aes, aeris (“bronze”) + -ūgō (forms nouns denoting superficial coatings). Or possibly from Late Latin arānea (originally spider's web, later coming to refer to skin diseases such as herpes, scabies, impetigo, etc.) crossed with rodere (“to gnaw”) into a Vu
Uncertain, probably from a Late Latin or Vulgar Latin roncus or ronchus, of Ancient Greek origin, or alternatively a root *runcus, from Latin runcō.
Probably from a derivative of Latin rebellāre or from arrovellare. Another possibility is Latin rubellus, diminutive of ruber.
From roffia (“dirt”), from Old High German hruf (“eschar, crust”). Cognate with Icelandic hrufla (“to scratch”), English ruffle. Alternatively from Vulgar Latin *rufianus, from rūfus (“red”).
From sabbia + -one or from Late Latin sablōnem, from Latin sabulōnem. Compare archaic French sablon.
Borrowed from Lombardic *sala (“hall”), from either Proto-Germanic *saliz or *salą (both meaning "house, hall").
From sale (“salt”) + -are (1ˢᵗ-conjugation verbal suffix), or from a Vulgar Latin *salāre, changed in conjugation from Latin salīre.
Borrowed from Latin sarcoma, from Ancient Greek σάρκωμα (sárkōma), from σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”) + -ωμα (-ōma, “process”) or from Ancient Greek σαρκόω (sarkóō), itself from σάρξ (sárx).
From s- + battere, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *exbattere, from Latin battuere.
From the adjective biado (alternatively biavo) from Late Latin blāvus, from Old High German blāo (whence also Italian blu via French), cognate with English blue. The s- is an intensifier.

Derived regressively from the verb scalzare, or possibly from a Vulgar Latin root *excalceus, itself either from a shortening of Latin excalceatus, or from ex- + calceus. From Old Italian schermugio (“skirmish”) (both with diminutive ending?). Alternatively both Italian forms might be derived from Old French escarmuche. Related to the verb schermire (“to protect, shield; to fence, swordfight”), stemming from Lombardic skirmen or Frankish *skirmijan (“to protect, defe
Borrowed from French écharpe, from Old French escharpe, from Frankish *skirpa (“bandoleer”), of either Germanic or Latin origin.
Formed from Latin secundus, or from Latin secundāre.
From Turkish saray or from Vulgar Latin serrāculum, from a late form of Latin serāre (“lock up, close”), from sera (“lock, bolt”).
From sotterra + -are, or possibly a Vulgar Latin *subterrāre, from Latin sub- + terra.

From s- + penzolo or penzolare. Alternatively possibly from s- (< Latin ex) + a Vulgar Latin root *pendiolāre, from *pendiolus, from pendulus, from Latin pendō, or *expendiolāre. Compare Romanian spânzura.
From sperare + -anza, or from Vulgar Latin spērantia, from Latin spērāns. Compare French espérance, Spanish esperanza, Portuguese esperança

Borrowed from a Germanic language, perhaps Gothic *𐍃𐍀𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌰 (*spaiha) or from a Frankish cognate, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”). Cognates include obsolete French épie (“spy”), Spanish espía (“spy”), English spy and German spähen (“to peek, to spy”).

parole.significato: to spy on, peep, peek, observe
parole.testo: From spia + -are, or from Vulgar Latin *spiāre, from Frankish *spehōn or a Gothic equivalent, from Proto-Germanic *spehōną (“to see, look”), from Proto-Indo-European *speḱ- (“to look”).

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; alternatively; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain. Possibly from Vulgar Latin *disperdicāre, from Latin disperdere, or from Vulgar Latin *dispergicāre, iterative of Latin dispergere, or alternatively from Vulgar Latin *exprecāre ("drive into ruin"), from Latin ex- + precāri.

Either from Vulgar Latin *extentāre, from Latin tentāre, or from s- (from Latin Latin ex-) + tentare (from Latin temptāre), or from Vulgar Latin *abstentāre, from Latin abstentum, from abstineō. Cognate with Friulian stentâ, Lombard stentà, Piedmontese stenté.

Borrowed from Old French estival, of which the etymology is disputed: either from Medieval Latin aestivālis (“summerly”), in place of Classical Latin aestīvus (whence also Italian estivo), from aestās (“summer”), or from tībiālis (“tibial, of the tibia”), from tībia. Cognate with Sicilian stivala.
From stoppa + -are or from Vulgar Latin *stuppāre, from Latin stuppa. Compare Venetan stupar, Sicilian stuppari, Romansh stuppar, French étouper, Old Spanish estopar, Romanian astupa.
Borrowed from Japanese 天麩羅 (てんぷら, tenpura), from Portuguese, ultimately from Latin, cognate with either temperare or tempo, tempora. See above for more.
From terra, or from Vulgar Latin *terraceus, from Latin terra. Related to terrazza. Cf. also terraccio, terracia. Compare Spanish terrazo.
From Latin texere, from Proto-Italic *teksō, either from Proto-Indo-European *tḗtḱ-ti or from *teḱ-se-ti, both from *teḱ- (“to beget, produce”).
Inherited from Late Latin tīmōnem, alteration of Classical Latin tēmōnem; alternatively, directly inherited into Italian from the Classical form, with pretonic /e/ > /i/.

parole.significato: to blank, shear, or trench (sheet metal)
parole.testo: Possibly from Vulgar Latin *trīnicāre, from trīnī + root of duplicō, or from an alternation of Latin truncāre.

parole.motivo_incerta: Uncertain; Possibly; or from; modello unc/uncertain
parole.testo: Uncertain; possibly from Arabic تَرْب (tarb, “bowels”), or from a Celtic root connected with Old Irish tarpán (“bunch of grapes”). Compare Spanish tripa and Portuguese tripa.

parole.motivo_incerta: Of uncertain origin; alternatively; or possibly

From unghia (“nail, claw”) + -ato, or from Late Latin ungulātus, from Latin ungula.

Venetan valís, Lombard valiza), from Medieval Latin valesia, valixia, from Late Latin valisia, possibly from Gaulish *valisia (“leather bag”), from Proto-Celtic *wal- (“to enclose, surround”), from Proto-Indo-European *welH-. Borrowed from Occitan vermelh, or from French vermeil, in either case from Vulgar Latin *vermiclus, syncopated from Latin vermiculus (“little worm”).

parole.significato: music played on a music video
parole.testo: From English video + English music, or from English music video.

Uncertain. Most sources originate it from Late Latin faluppa (“chaff, waste”) (from which also the doublet faloppa), influenced from/crossed with a derivate of Latin volvere. Other sources theorizes a sole derivation from volvere. Lastly, it may be related to/based on Old French (en)velopper, which
Uncertain, but possibly from Vulgar Latin *vincidus, itself likely derived from Latin vinciō (“tie, restrain”), or alternatively an alteration of viscido.
Inherited from Vulgar Latin *vīsitus, from Latin vīsus, or from a form *vīditus.
From Latin volō through a Vulgar Latin root *volia, or from voglio. Cf. also Romanian voie from root *volia

Inherited from Vulgar Latin *volta, from *volŭta (perhaps via *volvita (“a turn”)), from Latin volūta, feminine of volūtus, perfect passive participle of volvō. Also possibly from the past participle of volgere (volto), or from the verb voltare. Compare Spanish vuelta; cf. also Spanish bóveda, Frenc

parole.significato: raft (primitive vessel, modern emergency or sports craft)
parole.testo: From zatta, ultimately of Germanic origin. Alternatively, from Lombardic zattera, from Proto-West Germanic *tat(t)ur.
